section_summary: This section begins with diplomatic reporting on the March 1933 Sanriku earthquake and tsunami, including casualty estimates, the safety of American residents, and an exchange of condolences between the United States and Japan. It then contains records concerning the March 1934 Hakodate fire, a July 1930 typhoon in the Nagasaki district, and the devastating September 1934 typhoon in the Kansai region. The latter records cover American casualties, proposed Red Cross aid, presidential condolences, extensive industrial and port damage in Osaka and Kobe, and reconstruction of the Port of Osaka.

subfiles.title: Initial report of the Sanriku earthquake and tidal wave
subfiles.about: Reports the earthquake and tidal wave in northern Honshu and the known status of American citizens.
subfiles.summary: A severe earthquake centered in Iwate struck northern Honshu about 2:30 a.m., followed by a tidal wave and fires; preliminary figures: 15 dead, 300 missing, 110 injured, and none of 82 registered American residents known hurt.

subfiles.title: Revised earthquake casualty report
subfiles.about: Updates the casualty totals from the northern Honshu earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Revised incomplete official figures: 300 dead, 173 missing, 1,200 injured; the Embassy found no sign of American casualties.

subfiles.title: Authorization concerning losses in northern Honshu
subfiles.about: Extends an earlier authorization to losses caused by the recent northern Honshu earthquake.
subfiles.summary: State cites November telegrams and says the Embassy is similarly authorized concerning losses in the northern Honshu earthquake; the exact action isn't specified.

subfiles.title: Delivery of American condolences for the Sanriku disaster
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports delivery of the American Government's message of sympathy to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew conveyed American sympathy for deaths and losses in the Sanriku earthquake and tidal wave; Japan's Foreign Minister expressed deep appreciation.

subfiles.title: Further report on earthquake casualties and American residents
subfiles.about: Provides further casualty and property figures and reports no injuries to Americans.
subfiles.summary: No American injuries and foreign casualties unlikely, living outside the hardest-hit zones; revised totals: 1,500 dead, 950 missing, 340 injured, 10,800 houses damaged or destroyed.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on Japanese thanks
subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo despatch No. 320 concerning Japanese thanks for American sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Note that Tokyo despatch 320 transmitted Count Uchida's thanks for the Embassy's sympathy message after the northern Japan earthquake.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Japanese Foreign Minister's thanks
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a translated Japanese note thanking the United States for its expression of sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Grew referred to his March 6 telegram conveying American sympathy for the earthquake and tidal wave in northern Honshu. He enclosed the Foreign Minister's March 8 note thanking the Government and people of the United States.

subfiles.title: Count Uchida's note of thanks for earthquake sympathy
subfiles.from: Count Yasuya Uchida, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks the United States for its sympathy following the Sanriku earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Count Uchida, deeply moved by American sympathy over the Sanriku calamity, asks Grew to convey Japan's sincere thanks to the American government and people.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on Iwate and Miyagi relief
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a despatch concerning relief after the Iwate and Miyagi earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch 348 (April 1, 1933) on relief measures after the Iwate and Miyagi earthquake.

subfiles.title: Summary of the earthquake, tsunami, and initial relief measures
subfiles.about: Summarizes the destruction and early Japanese relief response after the northern Japan earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Submarine earthquake and eight-foot tidal wave devastated about 500 miles of coast, killing about 1,550 with nearly 1,000 missing; aircraft surveyed, destroyers searched for fishing boats, and the War Office, Emperor and Home Office gave funds or organized relief.

subfiles.title: Hakodate fire file jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the file concerning the destruction of Hakodate by fire.
subfiles.summary: The jacket opens the subject file for the March 1934 destruction of Hakodate. It bears the classification 894.48-HAKODATE.

subfiles.title: Initial report and condolences concerning the Hakodate fire
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Hakodate's destruction and the delivery of American condolences.
subfiles.summary: Grew called the Hakodate fire a major catastrophe and personally expressed U.S. condolences to Japan's Foreign Minister; press said the city was nearly destroyed with about 1,500 deaths, and American residents' status was unknown.

subfiles.title: American missionaries in fire-stricken Hakodate
subfiles.about: Identifies American residents of Hakodate and reports that their welfare was unknown.
subfiles.summary: Nearly all major Hakodate buildings except two wards burned; consular records list American missionaries Alice Cheney and Mary Collins, but damaged communications prevent confirming their welfare.

subfiles.title: Departmental consideration of a further Hakodate condolence message
subfiles.about: Considers whether another American message of condolence should be transmitted after the Hakodate fire.
subfiles.summary: Memo: the Ambassador already conveyed condolences for Hakodate; a Red Cross message could go through him, so no additional action is needed.

subfiles.title: Reduced estimate of Hakodate deaths
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a revised maximum estimate of deaths in the Hakodate fire.
subfiles.summary: Detailed information about the catastrophe remained unavailable. The latest reports reduced the estimated maximum loss of life to 1,000.

subfiles.title: Hull-Saito conversation on Japanese appreciation
subfiles.about: Records the Japanese Ambassador's delivery of thanks for American sympathy after the Hakodate fire.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Saito gives Hull a telegram from his Foreign Minister thanking the U.S. for sympathy after the Hakodate fire.

subfiles.title: Hirota's instruction to convey Japanese thanks
subfiles.about: Directs Saito to thank the Secretary of State for American sympathy over the Hakodate disaster.
subfiles.summary: Hirota reports Grew conveyed American sympathy March 22 and instructs Saito to express Japan's sincere appreciation to the Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Confirmation of no American casualties at Hakodate
subfiles.about: Confirms that no Americans were casualties of the Hakodate disaster.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reported that definite information had finally become available. No American casualties had occurred in the Hakodate fire.

subfiles.title: Memorandum opposing American relief for Hakodate
subfiles.about: Argues against presidential or public American relief contributions for Hakodate.
subfiles.summary: Memo calls a presidential relief initiative for Hakodate impracticable, questions the large 1933 American contribution, and warns Japanese resentment over the 1924 Exclusion Act might lead to rejection or suspicion it eased political guilt.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Hakodate relief correspondence
subfiles.about: Refers a private proposal concerning Hakodate relief to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: White House referral, signed by Marvin McIntyre, sends the Hakodate relief correspondence to State for consideration.

subfiles.title: McIntyre acknowledgment to Walter A. Conant
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Conant's proposal and promises to call it to President Roosevelt's attention.
subfiles.summary: McIntyre thanks Walter Conant for his March 22 letter and will bring the proposal to the President's attention.

subfiles.title: Conant proposal for presidential relief at Hakodate
subfiles.about: Urges President Roosevelt to undertake large-scale relief for Hakodate as an act of humanitarian leadership.
subfiles.summary: Conant argues generous relief for Hakodate would raise Roosevelt's prestige against Mussolini, Hitler and Stalin, given American food and clothing surpluses, and asks McIntyre to present it to him.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Hakodate mayor's letter of appreciation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the Hakodate Municipal Assembly's appreciation for American sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses the Hakodate mayor's letter conveying the Municipal Assembly's appreciation for the American Government's message of sympathy.

subfiles.title: Hakodate Municipal Assembly resolution of appreciation
subfiles.about: Asks the Ambassador to convey Hakodate's appreciation for the American inquiry and sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Mayor Sakamoto sends the Municipal Assembly's resolution appreciating the Ambassador's inquiry through the Foreign Office after the city's fire.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Harbin relief contributions for Hakodate
subfiles.about: Points to a Harbin despatch describing relief contributions for Hakodate.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Harbin despatch: Soviet, White Russian, Polish, Jewish, Japanese and individual American donors in Harbin contributed to Hakodate relief.

subfiles.title: Extract on Harbin contributions to Hakodate relief
subfiles.about: Reports relief contributions from Harbin following the Hakodate fire.
subfiles.summary: Extract: the March 21 Hakodate fire prompted many Harbin contributions, with Soviet, White Russian, Polish, Jewish and Japanese organizations giving and Americans contributing individually.

subfiles.title: Nagasaki typhoon file jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the file concerning the July 1930 typhoon at Nagasaki.
subfiles.summary: The jacket opens a subject file on the 1930 Nagasaki typhoon. Its date range begins July 21, 1930.

subfiles.title: Report on casualties and damage from the Nagasaki typhoon
subfiles.about: Reports casualties, damage, and the safety of Americans after the July 18 typhoon.
subfiles.summary: No Americans among about 350 killed in the Nagasaki typhoon; damage in the consular district was about 100 million yen, 20 million in Nagasaki Prefecture, and the consulate expects to request funds for urgent repairs.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with the American Red Cross on the typhoon
subfiles.from: Mr. Miller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Ernest P. Bicknell, American National Red Cross
subfiles.about: Records discussion of the July 18 typhoon in southern Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Miller read Bicknell the Nagasaki consul's report; Bicknell said the Red Cross got no request for typhoon aid and Japan declined outside aid for earlier floods, but asked for a copy.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Nagasaki typhoon telegram to the Red Cross
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Acting Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Ernest P. Bicknell, American National Red Cross
subfiles.about: Sends the Red Cross a copy of the American consul's typhoon telegram.
subfiles.summary: Peck confirms the morning's call and encloses the July 21 Nagasaki cablegram, with no further official typhoon communication from Japan.

subfiles.title: Red Cross acknowledgment of Nagasaki typhoon information
subfiles.from: Ernest P. Bicknell, American Red Cross
subfiles.to: Willys R. Peck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the consul's cablegram about the Nagasaki typhoon.
subfiles.summary: Bicknell thanks Peck for the Nagasaki typhoon cablegram and will keep it in the Red Cross disaster file.

subfiles.title: Osaka typhoon file jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the file concerning the September 1934 typhoon at Osaka.
subfiles.summary: File jacket opening the subject file on the 1934 Osaka typhoon, September 21, 1934.

subfiles.title: Authorization to express sympathy after the Osaka typhoon
subfiles.about: Authorizes an expression of sympathy if the Embassy considers the typhoon's severity sufficient.
subfiles.summary: Citing about 200 casualties and heavy damage, State authorizes the Embassy to express American sympathy if circumstances warrant and asks a telegraphic report.

subfiles.title: Safety of Americans in the Kobe-Osaka district
subfiles.about: Reports that no Americans were killed or injured in the Kobe-Osaka typhoon.
subfiles.summary: Donovan reports no Americans were killed or injured in the typhoon that struck Kobe and Osaka.

subfiles.title: Major casualty estimate and delivery of American sympathy
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports catastrophic losses and the Embassy's oral expression of sympathy to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reports put deaths above 1,000 and damage at several hundred million yen in Osaka, Hyogo and Kyoto; Neville conveyed American sympathy through the Foreign Ministry, and the Vice Minister expressed appreciation.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Osaka typhoon correspondence
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs staff
subfiles.about: Asks a Department official to handle an Osaka typhoon matter.
subfiles.summary: Internal routing note within Far Eastern Affairs on Osaka typhoon correspondence: "Would you handle?"

subfiles.title: Private inquiry concerning relatives in Kobe
subfiles.about: Requests information about a daughter and son-in-law believed to have been in Kobe during the typhoon.
subfiles.summary: Weinheimer says his daughter and her husband, Morris Weisenberg, were due in Kobe around the typhoon and asks about fatalities and their safety.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Tokyo concerning possible American Red Cross aid
subfiles.about: Requests advice on whether an American Red Cross contribution would be welcomed in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull transmitted John Barton Payne's request for guidance on whether the American Red Cross should contribute to relief through the Japanese Red Cross. The Embassy was cautioned not to appear overly eager or to press assistance that Japan might regard as politically motivated or unwelcome.

subfiles.title: Suggested cablegram on Red Cross assistance
subfiles.about: Drafts an inquiry about whether American Red Cross aid would be appropriate and welcome.
subfiles.summary: Draft cable: Payne sent sympathy to Prince Tokugawa and will soon visit Japan with an American delegation; it asks whether the Japanese Red Cross is doing relief and would welcome an American contribution.

subfiles.title: Embassy advice against a formal Red Cross contribution
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Advises that Japan appeared able and willing to manage typhoon relief without foreign Red Cross assistance.
subfiles.summary: Embassy advises against a formal Red Cross contribution: Japan has ample supplies, funds and organization, administers donations itself, and Neville thinks it prefers to bear relief and rehabilitation alone.

subfiles.title: Notice of the President's sympathy message to Emperor Hirohito
subfiles.about: Informs the Embassy of President Roosevelt's direct message of sympathy to the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: State supplies the text of the President's message to Emperor Hirohito expressing sympathy for Japan's suffering and distress.

subfiles.title: President Roosevelt's message to Emperor Hirohito
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.about: Conveys American sympathy for the catastrophic typhoon in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt tells Hirohito the American people were profoundly moved by the catastrophe and asks him to convey sympathy to those suffering.

subfiles.title: Emperor Hirohito's reply to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Thanks the President and American people for their sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Hirohito thanks Roosevelt and the American people warmly for their sympathy.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Hirohito's reply
subfiles.about: Forwards the Emperor's reply to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: White House referral slip, signed by Louis Howe, sends Hirohito's reply to State.

subfiles.title: Telegraphic copy of Hirohito's thanks
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, White House
subfiles.about: Provides a clear telegraphic copy of Hirohito's response to Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Telegraphic copy of Hirohito's thanks for Roosevelt's and the American people's sympathy.

subfiles.title: Departmental reply to John Barton Payne on Red Cross aid
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Barton Payne, American National Red Cross
subfiles.about: Provides the Embassy's advice concerning a proposed American Red Cross contribution.
subfiles.summary: Phillips tells John Barton Payne the Department sent his suggested inquiry to Tokyo and encloses the Chargé's reply that Japan prefers to administer relief and rehabilitation itself.

subfiles.title: Reply to family inquiry about the Weisenbergs
subfiles.from: Herbert C. Hengstler, Department of State
subfiles.about: Responds to an inquiry about Mr. and Mrs. Morris Weisenberg after the Kobe typhoon.
subfiles.summary: Hengstler reported that no American citizens were known to have been killed or injured in the September 21 typhoon at Kobe. He offered to ask the American consul to locate the Weisenbergs by telegram at Weinheimer's expense or by mail without charge, provided their full Kobe address was supplied.

subfiles.title: Survey of the September 21 typhoon in the Kansai district
subfiles.about: Surveys casualties and the extensive industrial and economic damage caused by the Kansai typhoon.
subfiles.summary: Donovan reported about 2,500 deaths, more than 8,000 injuries, extensive school collapses, flooding, and severe damage to factories in Osaka, Kobe, and neighboring prefectures. The report details losses to metal, chemical, textile, cotton, steel, and dockyard enterprises, while noting that rayon and woolen mills escaped relatively lightly. Official figures listed 2,508 dead and 8,455 injured, with total damage across the affected prefectures provisionally estimated at one billion yen.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on voluntary Osaka port report
subfiles.about: Notes receipt of a voluntary report describing typhoon damage at the Port of Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Note on Kobe's voluntary October 23, 1934 report of typhoon damage at the Port of Osaka; no departmental action needed.

subfiles.title: Typhoon Damage at the Port of Osaka, Japan
subfiles.from: Robert Mills McClintock, Vice Consul, Kobe; approved by Howard Donovan
subfiles.about: Documents typhoon damage, reconstruction, and the restoration of normal operations at the Port of Osaka.
subfiles.summary: McClintock describes a 135-mile-per-hour typhoon and fifteen-foot storm surge that wrecked vessels, destroyed the Great Pier, damaged warehouses and customs facilities, crippled the Sakurajima coal docks, and halted port operations for nearly a week. Municipal and national authorities began rebuilding piers, sheds, and breakwaters, while salvage work and temporary reductions in port charges encouraged shipping to return. By mid-October operations were nearly normal, although lighter shortages, berth congestion, and damaged coal-handling facilities remained.
